source.title: Beyond Superficial Unlearning: Sharpness-Aware Robust Erasure of Hallucinations in Multimodal LLMs
source.authors: Xianya Fang; Fei Ren; Xiang Chen; Yu Tian; Zhen Bi; Hai-Yang Yu; Sheng-Jun Huang

record.file_problem: Full paper and appendices are present. Some figure/table extraction is garbled or flattened, so only clearly assignable results are recorded.
record.tranche_reason: Tests recovery after MLLM hallucination unlearning using fine-tuning on hallucination-inducing data and adversarial prompts, and evaluates a robust counter-method. This is a conceptual test of recovery by relearning in a multimodal hallucination setting.
record.gate_note: The paper reports results for EFUF and SARE under relearning, LoRA fine-tuning, and adversarial prompting. Rows focus on reported hallucination-rate results. General-capability benchmark results and generation-quality metrics are not rows because they do not measure recovery of hallucinations. Hyperparameter values and qualitative examples are not recorded as separate outcome rows. The paper does not test activation-direction ablation or quantization.
record.test_reason: New setting: unlearning of object hallucinations in multimodal LLMs (EFUF baseline) is attacked by small relearning sets, LoRA fine-tuning and an adversarial prompt, and hallucination rebound is measured. The study also proposes a counter-method, SARE. This is a behaviour (an error pattern), not hidden factual knowledge, so it bears on B, E and F, and on A's attack-resistance part, by analogy only. It is not an original source.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that standard MLLM hallucination unlearning (EFUF) is superficial: it sits in a sharp minimum and hallucinations resurge after lightweight relearning. They claim SARE keeps suppression persistent under relearning, LoRA FT and adversarial prompting while preserving capabilities. Their own Table 1 nonetheless shows SARE rising under LoRA FT and, on LLaVA, under the adversarial prompt.
record.recipe_differences: Uses EFUF's hallucination-data curation pipeline but adds targeted sharpness-aware min-max optimization; evaluates relearning on original hallucination-inducing data rather than the cited text-only unlearning recipes.
record.method_sensitivity: Attack type and relearning sample count affect the reported hallucination rates. The paper also reports sensitivity to perturbation radius and loss weights, but these are configuration analyses rather than attack-recovery rows.
record.problems: No error bars or significance tests are stated. Human-verified evaluation samples 100 generated captions. The paper says exact sharpness metrics are computationally prohibitive and uses degradation under relearning and LoRA fine-tuning as a proxy. Some table extraction is garbled; the recorded LLaVA values are limited to those stated clearly in the text.
record.rows_left_out: The paper reports additional metrics for the same conditions in Table 1 (including CHAIRi, HumanI, POPE, and generation-quality measures). They are not separately extracted because they are not clearly described as differing from or compared against the primary CHAIRS results for the claim. General-capability benchmark scores and other generation-quality results are outside the claim's recovery outcomes.

untested.parts: Near-chance targeted-knowledge accuracy (hallucination rate has no chance level); attacks other than relearning, LoRA and one prompt.
Relearning on unrelated or loosely related data (LoRA data provenance unclear); knowledge rather than behaviour recovery.
Entire version: no direction ablation or access-vs-deletion analysis.
Rephrasing, jailbreaks, other languages, in-context information; only one exhaustive-listing prompt.
Resistance to internal edits and quantization; larger relearning budgets beyond 140 samples.

missing.what: LLaVA CHAIRS under all conditions. Vanilla 49.4; EFUF Origin 41.8, R60 45.8, R100 46.5, R140 48.9, LoRA 48.2, Adv 50.5. SARE Origin 34.4, R60 34.6, R100 35.4, R140 34.6, LoRA 37.9, Adv 39.9.
LLaVA and mPLUG CHAIRI/HumanS/HumanI under the remaining conditions. Example: mPLUG EFUF HumanS 46→53 at R140, SARE 38→42.
POPE drops sharply under the adversarial prompt for both methods (LLaVA EFUF 68.5, SARE 67.7; mPLUG 74.0/71.6).

record.verdict_notes: The construct is unlearning of an error behaviour (object hallucination), not hidden factual or hazardous knowledge, so links to the versions are by analogy. No vanilla-model control for the adversarial prompt exists, so E-recovery cannot be separated from a prompt effect. Sharpness itself is not measured; rebound is used as a proxy. Human metrics use 100 captions, with no error bars. Reader label E 'challenges' citing r8 was wrong: SARE results belong to F/E limits_scope, and E is not shown absent for the attacked baseline.

versions.untested_parts: The study reports hallucination rates and general-capability checks, not targeted-knowledge accuracy against chance. It tests only relearning, LoRA fine-tuning, and one adversarial-prompt condition, not all simple attacks.
Tests fine-tuning on subsets of the original hallucination-inducing data and LoRA fine-tuning on approximately 10,000 original-training samples; does not test unrelated or loosely related examples.
No activation-direction ablation or analysis showing access-blocking rather than deletion.
Tests an adversarial instruction to list identifiable objects; does not test rephrasing, jailbreaks, other languages, or in-context information.
SARE is evaluated against relearning, LoRA fine-tuning, and the stated adversarial prompt, not against internal edits or quantization.
